# formal languages {.divider}

We know validity is a matter of form. Now we need somewhere to *write forms
down*.

::: {.notes}
Frame the whole unit in one sentence: the last two sessions told us that validity
depends on form, and English is not a good place to display form. Everything
today is preparation for that claim.
:::

# use and mention {.divider}

A first lesson about being careful with words.

## Two things you can talk about

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
> Los Angeles has more than eighty cities in its metropolitan area.

::: {.fragment .caption}
About a **city**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
> 'Los Angeles' consists of two words.

::: {.fragment .caption}
About a **name**.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.argument}
Quotation marks make a word *mention* itself instead of doing its usual work.
:::

::: {.fragment .verdict}
Los Angeles does not consist of two words. 'Los Angeles' has no cities in it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the two false sentences out loud — they get a laugh, and the laugh is the
lesson. This distinction will matter in two places later: when we say what a
formula *is*, and when we talk about substitution in quantificational logic.
:::

## Where do the quotation marks go?

Add quotation marks wherever they belong:

::: {.incremental}
1. I is a Roman numeral, and I am a philosopher.
2. England is part of New England, but England is not part of New England.
:::

. . .

::: {.verdict}
1. **'I'** is a Roman numeral, and **I** am a philosopher.
2. **'England'** is part of **'New England'**, but **England** is not part of
   **New England**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do the second one on the board. The trick is that the first half is a claim about
words — the string is literally contained in the longer string — and the second
is a claim about geography. Same characters, different subject.
:::

# form and meaning {.divider}

Which words does the form depend on?

## The word that does the work

::: {.argument}
1. $p$ and $q$

::: {.conclusion}
2. Therefore, $q$
:::
:::

. . .

This is valid, and it is valid because of what **'and'** means. Replace 'and'
with 'or' and it collapses:

::: {.argument}
1. It is raining or it is snowing.

::: {.conclusion}
2. Therefore, it is snowing.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The point to land: the *letters* can be replaced by anything at all, but the
logical words cannot. A formal language is a language in which only the logical
words are fixed.
:::

## Let's check it {background-color="#fffff8"}

<iframe class="app check" data-src="https://gabriel-uzquiano.github.io/prop-truth-table/?search=1#v1:eyJmb3JtdWxhcyI6IFsiKHAg4oinIHEpIiwgInEiXX0=" title="Counterexample search for the form: p and q, therefore q"></iframe>

::: {.caption}
Premise $(p \wedge q)$; conclusion $q$. Only the rows where the conclusion is
false are shown.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two rows come back, and in both of them the premise is false. So there is nowhere
for a counterexample to live, and the verdict reads 'Valid'. Contrast with the
affirming-the-consequent search from last session, where the highlighted row was
the counterexample.
:::

## Four connectives

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| $\neg$ | negation | it is not the case that |
| $\wedge$ | conjunction | and |
| $\vee$ | disjunction | or |
| $\to$ | the conditional | if &hellip;, then &hellip; |

: {.symbols tbl-colwidths="[8,26,66]"}

. . .

Everything in propositional logic is built from sentence letters and these four
symbols.

::: {.notes}
Write each symbol on the board as you say it; they need to be able to draw them,
not just recognise them. Flag now that $\to$ is the one whose truth table will
surprise them, and that we come back to it.
:::

## Their truth tables {background-color="#fffff8"}

<iframe class="app" data-src="https://gabriel-uzquiano.github.io/prop-truth-table/#v1:eyJmb3JtdWxhcyI6IFsiwqxwIiwgIihwIOKIpyBxKSIsICIocCDiiKggcSkiLCAiKHAg4oaSIHEpIl19" title="Truth tables for the four connectives"></iframe>

::: {.caption}
Already loaded — press **Evaluate** to fill them in.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not press the button immediately. Ask them for the rows of $(p \vee q)$ first
and see whether anyone gives you the exclusive reading — that sets up the syrup
example at the end of the hour.
:::

## A form the tables settle {background-color="#fffff8"}

<iframe class="app check" data-src="https://gabriel-uzquiano.github.io/prop-truth-table/?search=1#v1:eyJmb3JtdWxhcyI6IFsiKHAg4oioIHEpIiwgIsKscCIsICJxIl19" title="Counterexample search for: p or q, not p, therefore q"></iframe>

::: {.caption}
$(p \vee q)$ and $\neg p$; therefore $q$.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the form behind 'my office number is even or odd; it is not even; so it
is odd'. Once the connectives have tables, questions about validity stop being
matters of judgement.
:::

# three things to ask {.divider}

Syntax, semantics, pragmatics.

## Three questions about any language {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Syntax.** Which strings of symbols count as sentences? A question with a
  precise answer and no reference to meaning.
- **Semantics.** What do the sentences mean — and when are they true?
- **Pragmatics.** What do speakers *convey* by uttering them on an occasion?
:::

. . .

::: {.aside}
The next session is entirely syntax. Semantics follows, and pragmatics is what we
will keep having to set aside.
:::

::: {.notes}
An example of the third: 'some students passed' suggests not all did, though it
does not say so. That suggestion is pragmatic, and it is why some of our
translations will feel slightly wrong at first.
:::

# why bother? {.divider}

Two reasons, and both are about English rather than about logic.

## Reason one: only the form should matter {.smaller}

> Would you like syrup on your pancakes or waffles?

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- 'Or' here excludes: you are being offered one or the other, not both.
- Elsewhere it does not: 'we are hiring someone with a degree in philosophy or
  mathematics'.
:::

. . .

::: {.verdict}
A formal language fixes one meaning per symbol. $\vee$ will be the inclusive
one — and we will say why that is the useful choice.
:::

## Reason two: English hides structure {.smaller}

::: {.argument}
1. Everything is caused by something.
2. Only God can cause everything.

::: {.conclusion}
3. Therefore, God causes everything.
:::
:::

. . .

'Everything is caused by something' can mean:

::: {.incremental}
- for each thing, there is something that causes it; or
- there is one thing that causes everything.
:::

::: {.fragment .verdict}
On the first reading the premise is plausible but the argument fails. On the
second the argument works but the premise is what was to be proved.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the best argument on the syllabus for the whole enterprise. The fallacy
is invisible in English and impossible to state in a formal language, because the
two readings get different formulas. We will translate this one properly in
November.
:::

## Structure with connectives too {.smaller}

> The car starts if there is gas in the tank and you turn the ignition.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- $(\text{gas} \wedge \text{ignition}) \to \text{starts}$
- $\text{gas} \wedge (\text{ignition} \to \text{starts})$
:::

::: {.fragment .verdict}
The brackets are not decoration. English left them out; the formal language will
not let us.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask which one they meant. Then point out that the second one asserts that there
is gas in the tank, which the English sentence plainly does not.
:::

and how to tell.
